title: Blender, stand mixer or stick blender: safe teardown
summary: Get the brushed high-speed motor, its fan and bearings, speed switches and speed control, the thermal cut-out and the cord out of a blender, plus a geared head from a stand mixer. The blade assembly is the main danger: it stays razor sharp, so handle it only in cut-resistant gloves and never put a hand into the jar or onto the drive socket while it is plugged in.

steps.text: Unplug the blender, keep the plug where you can see it, and lift the jar off the base. If it was running, give the motor time to cool. Vitamix says to unplug before taking any part on or off (Vitamix 5200 manual).
steps.warn: Never put fingers into the jar or onto the drive socket while it is plugged in. A blade can start if a switch is bumped.

steps.text: Put on cut-resistant gloves before you touch the blade. On jars with a threaded nut or skirt underneath (Oster), turn the jar upside down, unscrew the nut and lift out the blade by its hub, then the sealing ring. The maker's manual shows the sealing ring, blade and nut going on in that order, with the nut tightened clockwise (Oster push-button manual). If the blade is held by a nut you can't turn without your hand near the edges, leave the blade in the jar.
steps.warn: Hold the blade only by its hub or base, never along the edges, even with gloves on. Wrap it in thick cloth and tape it before you put it down.

steps.text: Vitamix-type bases: lift off the rubber pad round the drive socket, put a 5/64 in hex key into the small hole at the socket's base at an angle and turn it left only until the socket comes free. It sits on a square nut (iFixit Vitamix drive socket).
steps.warn: Don't loosen the screw too far: it can drop down into the motor.

steps.text: Turn the base over on a towel. Undo the base screws (some hide under rubber feet; some need security bits) and release any side clips. The Blendtec Total base comes off after two recessed Phillips screws and four clips (iFixit Blendtec). Lift the cover but don't touch any wire yet.

Wait at least 5 minutes since you unplugged it. Check your meter on a battery first. Find every capacitor: on a control board, in a small mains filter like the Blendtec's (iFixit Blendtec), or a round or oval can on the motor if it has one. Discharge each one rated over 50 V, or with no readable rating, with a resistor tool, measure DC volts across it, then check the meter on the battery again. Under 1 V is safe; clip a wire across the big ones (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: Never measure first, and never short a capacitor with a screwdriver.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring. Pull the spade connectors off by their plugs, not the wires. Lift out the control board, switch panel and speed dial whole. On a KitchenAid Classic, first unhook the control board spring with long-nose pliers and back out the two speed adjusting screws (KitchenAid Classic manual). The Blendtec board sits on moulded brackets with no screws (iFixit Blendtec); the KitchenAid Classic's triac is one small screw on the motor's bearing bracket (KitchenAid Classic manual).

Find the motor's overheat protection: a thermistor taped to the stator in the Blendtec (iFixit Blendtec), or a cut-out or reset button in others (Vitamix 5200 manual). If it is wired in series with the motor, leave it fitted to the motor instead of cutting it out. Otherwise cut its leads, leaving long tails. Never bridge it with wire, never heat it to test it, and never make a salvaged one the only protection.

Blendtec-type motors: hold the shaft with a 3/8 in hex key in the spline end, undo the nut at the fan end with a wrench, and lift off the fan (iFixit Blendtec). Then take out the brush housings and the screws or studs holding the motor, and lift out the stator and rotor. Keep the bearings on the shaft.
steps.warn: Wipe up brush dust with a damp cloth. Don't blow it about: it is fine carbon that conducts electricity.

steps.text: Stand mixers: take the bowl and any attachments off first (KitchenAid Classic manual). Lay the mixer in a padded cradle or on a folded cloth, then remove the end cover and trim band screws. Loosen the hinge-pin set screw and drive the hinge pin out with a drift punch to free the head from the pedestal. Tap off the drip ring, drive out the groove pin and pry the planetary off its shaft with two screwdrivers (KitchenAid Classic manual). Slide the cord's strain relief out of its slot.
steps.warn: Wear safety glasses when you drive pins with a punch and hammer. Rest the head on a towel so it can't roll off the bench.

steps.text: Open the stand mixer's gear case over a tray. Scoop the grease into a lidded jar and keep it. Lift out the worm gear bracket, bevel gears and planetary as sets. On the New Gen design the motor comes out after two screws, and its pinion and the first-stage gear are a matched pair (KitchenAid New Gen manual).

Stick blenders: press the release buttons to take off the blade shaft, pry off the speed-dial cap and undo the screws beneath it (iFixit Breville BSB510). If the case is welded shut, clamp it and saw round it just above the release buttons, stopping when you reach the metal motor (iFixit Breville BSB510).
steps.warn: Clamp the handle in a vice or to the bench. Never hold it in your hand while you saw. Wear safety glasses and keep your other hand clear of the saw's path.

steps.text: Once the stick blender is open, look for capacitors on its board (the Westinghouse board has a safety capacitor and two ceramic ones: iFixit Westinghouse stick mixer). Check your meter on a battery, discharge any capacitor rated over 50 V, or with no readable rating, with a resistor tool, measure DC volts across it, then check the meter on the battery again. Touch nothing on the board until it reads under 1 V, and leave a wire across the big ones.
Cut the cord off at the case, leaving it as long as you can, and keep the plug.
Test the motor (see the notes and test_motor) before you carry it far. Label every part OK or BAD.
steps.warn: For a run test, clamp the motor down, cover its terminals, plug in through an RCD (GFCI), keep hands and hair clear of the fan, and run it only briefly.

notes:
## Before you strip it

A working blender or stand mixer is worth more whole if you have mains power or a generator. A Vitamix 5200 is rated 120 V, 11.5 A (Vitamix 5200 manual), which is about 1.4 kW running (120 V x 11.5 A), so size a generator or inverter for at least that. Check that the jar and blade are sound: Vitamix says never run it with damaged blades (Vitamix 5200 manual).

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Motor.** A high-speed motor; the Blendtec and Westinghouse ones have carbon brushes (iFixit Blendtec, iFixit Westinghouse stick mixer), and the KitchenAid Classic's brushes run in brass inserts (KitchenAid Classic manual). The KitchenAid Classic's is a universal motor; its maker says that design runs on 50 or 60 Hz AC only (KitchenAid Classic manual). The Blendtec Total's is rated 1,560 W and spins at 28,000 rpm, with carbon brushes that wear out before the rest of the motor (iFixit Blendtec). The Vitamix 5200 has about 2 peak horsepower (Vitamix 5200 manual). Where you have mains, it may be able to drive a grinder, a sander, a fan or a small workshop tool, but it is far too fast for most jobs without a belt or gear reduction. Blender motors are built for short runs: Vitamix says its machine overheats if it runs too long at a low speed (Vitamix 5200 manual). Run a salvaged one in short bursts and let it cool. A universal motor has no magnets, so it is no use as a generator (see test_motor). Worn brushes: see repair_motor_brushes; KitchenAid reuses Classic brushes longer than 5/16 in (KitchenAid Classic manual).
- **Fan.** The Blendtec and KitchenAid New Gen motors carry a cooling fan on the shaft (iFixit Blendtec, KitchenAid New Gen manual). Keep it on the motor.
- **Bearings.** Blendtec's rotor runs in two ball bearings reported as size 608RS (iFixit Blendtec), the same size as skateboard bearings. Spin one by hand: rough or gritty means scrap it.
- **Speed control.** The KitchenAid Classic controls speed with a triac phase-control circuit on a heat sink, worked by a centrifugal governor and a board of contact switches (KitchenAid Classic manual). Keep the triac as a spare (test it as on the thyristor card). The board only works with its own governor, so don't count on reusing it whole.
- **Switches and speed dial.** The Vitamix 5200 has an on/off switch, a high/variable switch and a speed dial (Vitamix 5200 manual). Useful spares for any mains tool within their rating.
- **Thermal protection.** The Blendtec's thermistor shuts the motor off at 130 °C (iFixit Blendtec); Vitamix 220/240 V machines have a reset button underneath (Vitamix 5200 manual). A continuity reading doesn't prove a salvaged one will still trip. Never heat one to test it, never bridge one, and never make a salvaged one the only protection in anything you build.
- **Stand mixer gearbox.** A worm gear, bevel gears and a planetary in a sealed case. The Classic's attachment hub is driven off the same gears (KitchenAid Classic manual), so a whole head with its motor is a slow, strong drive where mains exists. Keep the gears in sets with their grease. Some New Gen units have a plastic transmission housing, which KitchenAid recommends replacing with a magnesium one (KitchenAid New Gen manual). Magnesium burns very hot, so never grind, drill or heat a metal housing (see skill_fire_starting).
- **Cord and plug.** Oster's are polarized (Oster push-button manual); the Vitamix 5200 has a three-prong earthed cord (Vitamix 5200 manual). Good for repairs and extension leads (see repair_extension_cord).
- **Glass jar.** A measuring jug or storage jar, if uncracked.

## Testing what you got out

- **Motor windings.** Take the wires off and measure ohms. KitchenAid gives about 1.5–2.0 Ω for each good stator coil on 100–120 V Classic mixers and 8–18 Ω on 220–240 V ones; zero means shorted, OL means open (KitchenAid Classic manual). Then measure from each wire to the metal frame: anything but OL means scrap it.
- **Brushes.** Check length and wear, and that they slide freely in their holders.
- **Run test.** Only through an RCD (GFCI), clamped down, terminals covered, fan clear. Keep any bench DC test at 30 V or less.

## Variations

- **Vitamix 5200.** About 2 peak hp, 120 V, 50/60 Hz, 11.5 A. Its overload protection shuts the motor off when it overheats; 120 V machines reset after the switch has been off for up to 45 minutes (Vitamix 5200 manual). The drive socket is a separate part held by a screw through a small hole (iFixit Vitamix drive socket).
- **Blendtec Total.** 1,560 W, 13 A, digital controls, a mechanical power switch at the back, an inductive speed sensor and a clear-coated logic board (iFixit Blendtec).
- **Oster push-button blenders.** Glass or plastic jar, sealing ring, blade and a threaded jar nut or skirt; the maker says the drive is all metal (Oster push-button manual).
- **KitchenAid Classic (for example KSM150).** Universal motor, centrifugal governor, triac phase control and contact-switch control board; the gear case holds 6 oz of grease (KitchenAid Classic manual).
- **KitchenAid New Gen (for example KP26M1X).** Units before date code WL46 have a 53-tooth gear and 8-tooth motor, later ones 60 and 10; the sets don't mix (KitchenAid New Gen manual).
- **Stick blenders.** The Breville BSB510 is rated 700 W, 220–240 V, and its case is welded, so it has to be sawn open; its blade shaft can't be taken apart without destructive or special tools (iFixit Breville BSB510). The Westinghouse 800 W stick mixer has a 500 g brushed motor with brushes reachable from the sides, and its circuit board is soldered to the motor (iFixit Westinghouse stick mixer).

## What to leave

- Blade assemblies, unless you are fixing another blender of the same make. Tape and wrap any you keep.
- Stick blender blade shafts: they can't be taken apart without destructive or special tools (iFixit Breville BSB510).
- Cracked jars, plastic housings and logic boards with nothing you can name on them.
- A motor with burnt windings or a burnt commutator.
